turns.text: What do you remember most vividly about your first night after arriving in Beidahuang from Shanghai?

The train dropped us at a station that barely deserved the name, and the cold hit me sharper than anything I’d ever felt. My coat from Shanghai was thin, useless against the wind that crawled through every seam. That first night, I lay on a wooden bunk in a long, drafty barracks, listening to the wind rattle the windowpanes and the unfamiliar voices around me. The air smelled of damp straw and something metallic, maybe from the stoves that never seemed to warm the room. I remember lying awake, my legs cramped from the journey, the ache in my back already starting, and feeling the weight of distance — not just from home, but from the person I’d been before stepping off that train. I kept my suitcase close, one hand on the latch, as if I might need to run. The darkness outside was absolute, no city lights, only the muffled sound of someone crying into their pillow a few beds away.

The way you describe clutching your suitcase and listening to someone cry makes the loneliness and fear feel so immediate. When you woke up that next morning, what was the first thing you saw or did that made you realize how different your life was going to be?

I woke to the sound of a whistle and boots thumping on the bare floorboards. The room was gray with dawn light, and I could see my breath when I sat up. My fingers were stiff, and I fumbled with the buttons on my coat. We were herded outside right away, into a yard where the snow crunched underfoot and the horizon seemed to go on forever, just flat land and scrubby trees. Someone handed me a shovel with a splintered handle, and I remember staring at the calluses on the hands of the locals, realizing mine were soft and useless. The work started before I’d even washed my face — breaking up frozen earth for a ditch that seemed to have no end. My boots filled with snow, and I kept thinking about how at home, my mother would be boiling eggs for breakfast, the smell of soy sauce and scallions filling the kitchen. Here, my stomach grumbled as we worked in silence, the only sound the scrape of shovels and the wind. In that moment, city life felt like a story I’d read in another language.

That first morning, I remember how the cold seemed to seep into my bones, but the real shock was in my hands. By midday, the skin split in places I hadn’t even known could crack. I kept looking down at them, raw and clumsy, and feeling embarrassed every time I dropped the shovel or had to stop to blow on my fingers. There was no space for weakness; the older women worked beside me, barely glancing my way, their movements practiced and quick. I felt invisible and exposed at the same time. At lunch, we sat on overturned buckets, eating a thin porridge that tasted faintly of ashes. I watched the steam rise from the bowl and tried to imagine warmth, but it felt like something I’d left behind in Shanghai. That’s when I realized the city wasn’t just far away — it might as well have been a different world.

The detail about your hands splitting and the taste of ash in the porridge makes the physical and emotional distance from home so real. When you saw the older women working beside you with such practiced movements, did you ever try to talk with them, or did you feel a barrier between you and the locals?

At first, I hardly spoke to them except when absolutely necessary. Their dialect was thick, and I stumbled over the words, afraid of sounding foolish. They didn’t seem interested in conversation, just getting through the day. Sometimes, I caught them glancing at my awkward grip on the shovel or the way I flinched from the cold, and I could feel their judgment. Once, during a break, I tried to ask one of them how she kept her hands from cracking so badly. She just shrugged and held up her palms, rough as tree bark, and said, “You get used to it.” There was no warmth in her voice, just a matter-of-fact acceptance. After that, I mostly kept to myself, listening more than talking, watching how they moved, how they layered their clothes, how they never wasted energy. The gulf between us felt as wide as the fields.

I learned quickly that silence was safer. The locals had their own rhythm, their own jokes I couldn’t follow. When they talked among themselves, their laughter sounded like it belonged to another life, one I couldn’t touch. I tried once to share a piece of candy I’d saved from the train, thinking it might bridge the gap, but the woman I offered it to just looked at me, then turned away. There was a sense that I was soft, spoiled, an outsider who didn’t know how to survive. I felt their eyes on me when I stumbled or lagged behind, but no one offered advice unless it was barked as a correction. I stopped expecting kindness and started copying their movements instead—how they wrapped their scarves, how they bent their knees to save their backs. I watched, learned, and kept my head down. The barrier wasn’t just language; it was a lifetime of difference packed into every gesture.

The moment when you offered candy and were turned away really stands out—it sounds like even small gestures could be misunderstood. Did you ever find comfort or connection with anyone during those early months, or did you feel isolated the whole time?

Mostly, I felt alone, especially in the fields and at night. But there were small moments that softened the edges. One evening, after a long day, I sat on the steps outside the barracks, rubbing ointment on my cracked hands. Another girl from Shanghai sat down beside me, silent at first, then quietly slid her jar of balm toward me. We didn’t say much—we just looked out at the empty land, sharing the cold. Sometimes, in the evenings, a few of us city kids would huddle together on someone’s bunk, trading stories about home or quietly singing old songs under our breath. Those moments didn’t erase the loneliness, but they made it possible to keep going. It wasn’t real comfort, not like family, but it was a kind of fragile connection—like a thread you grip when everything else feels like it’s slipping away.

The thread was thin, but I clung to it. There were nights when I lay awake listening to the wind, and the only thing that kept the fear from swallowing me was the sound of another girl’s breathing just a few feet away. Sometimes, when the work was finished and the lights were out, we’d whisper about what we missed—rice cakes, the taste of hot tea, the sound of the trams in the city. In those whispers, I heard my own longing echoed back, and it made the barracks feel a little less empty. We didn’t dare talk about our hopes for the future; that felt dangerous, almost traitorous. But sharing memories, even quietly, was a kind of rebellion against the emptiness. I never let myself fully trust anyone, not with secrets, but I leaned on the small kindnesses—an extra scrap of cloth for a bandage, a smile when someone managed to get a letter from home. It wasn’t friendship the way I’d known it, but it was enough to keep despair from settling in my bones.

Those whispered memories of home and the little acts of care sound like lifelines in a world that wanted you to be tough and silent. When someone did receive a letter from home, how did it affect the mood in the barracks, both for the person who got the letter and for everyone else?

When a letter arrived, it was like a tiny flare in the darkness—everyone noticed, even if we pretended not to. The person who got the letter would clutch it tightly, sometimes reading it over and over in the dim light, lips moving silently. For a little while, you could see something different in their eyes—a kind of warmth, or maybe just the relief of being remembered. The rest of us felt a strange mix of hope and envy. We’d listen for the sound of paper rustling, wondering if there might be news from our own families next time. Sometimes, if the letter was happy, the person would share a line or two—a description of a festival back home, or a joke from a younger sibling. But if it was bad news, the silence around their bunk got heavier, and we all felt it, even if nothing was said. The letters made the distance feel both smaller and larger at once.

I remember watching someone trace the characters with her finger, as if touching the ink could bring her family closer. There were nights when she’d tuck the letter under her pillow and sleep with her face turned to the wall. For me, those letters were a reminder that the world outside the fields still existed, but also a reminder of what I’d lost. Sometimes I’d lie awake, replaying the last words my mother had said to me before I left, trying to hold onto the sound of her voice. When a letter came for someone else, it hurt—a twist in my chest I tried to ignore. But it also sparked a quiet defiance in me: I would not let myself be erased, no matter how far away I was. Even if my hands were cracked and my body ached, I was still someone’s daughter, someone’s sister. The letters kept that part of me alive.

The image of someone tracing the characters with her finger really lingers—it’s such a physical way to hold onto a connection. Did you ever write letters home yourself, and if so, what did you choose to share or hide from your family about your life in Beidahuang?
